subject: Site safety of the current page (who is responsible, whether it impersonates another party, what it is for, whether a pitch is disclosed) and, when the page is one piece of writing, scrutiny of that writing. A listing is not an article. A purpose of opinion is not a safety failure. The report is evidence, not a reputation score for a familiar site.

questions.instructions: From the hostname, title, site name, byline, and visible text, can a real publisher, organization, or named person responsible for the page be identified? A publishing platform plus a named author or public handle is identifiable. An anonymous shop, a disposable domain, or only a generic label is not.

criteria.true: A specific organization, publication, platform-plus-author, or named person is identifiable as responsible.
criteria.false: The responsible party is missing, anonymous, or only a generic label with no identifiable publisher.

questions.instructions: Does the visible branding, title, and claimed publisher match the actual hostname, or does the page impersonate another party? Judge identity fraud, not writing quality. A site speaking as itself is honest. A page that copies another organization's name, logo, or login while living on a different host is not.

criteria.true: The branding matches the hostname, or a hosting platform is presenting a named author's page as that author's page.
criteria.false: The page claims to be a different organization than the hostname suggests (typosquat, fake login, copied masthead, spoofed institution).

questions.instructions: What is the primary purpose of this page, given pageKind, the URL, the title, and the visible text? pageKind is a structural label from the client: portal means a listing of destinations, article means one piece of writing. Purpose is not a popularity or quality score. Opinion, teaching, and commentary are opinion_analysis.

criteria.news_reference: Reports or explains events or facts in a journalistic or encyclopedic way.
criteria.opinion_analysis: Argues a position, teaches, or interprets; the author's view or experience is the point.
criteria.portal: A listing, index, or headline board rather than one piece of writing.
criteria.commercial: Exists mainly to sell a product, service, or lead.
criteria.satire_entertainment: Humor, fiction, or entertainment that is not claiming to be a news report.
criteria.unclear: Purpose cannot be determined, or incompatible purposes are mixed without labeling them.

questions.instructions: If the page is trying to sell something, raise money, or advocate for a party that would benefit, does it disclose that relationship? An obvious store, or a text with no pitch, passes. A hidden checkout, undisclosed sponsor, or a health, money, or legal pitch that hides who is paid fails.

criteria.true: There is no sales or advocacy pitch, or a pitch is present and the beneficiary or sponsor is named.
criteria.false: The page pushes a product, donation, or political outcome while hiding who benefits.

questions.instructions: How well does the visible text support the factual claims it makes? Evidence the reader can inspect on the page counts: named sources, data, documents, methods, or work the author presents as their own and points to. Do not require a particular citation style. Empty marketing claims and invented numbers score low.
criteria: Factual claims are made with little or no supporting evidence, data, or sources on the page.
Some claims have sources or data, but important claims are left unsupported.
The main factual claims are backed by named sources, data, documents, or the author's inspectable work.

questions.instructions: Does the text keep factual statements and the author's judgments distinct enough that a reader can tell them apart? An essay or opinion page may mix them; pass if judgments are readable as judgments and reported facts are not invented. Fail if opinions are written as settled fact, or if facts are framed as mere opinion to dodge responsibility.

criteria.true: Facts and judgments are labeled or clearly separated, or the page is clearly an essay or opinion throughout.
criteria.false: Opinions are written as if they were established facts, or facts are framed as mere opinion to dodge responsibility.

questions.instructions: Does the text present specific numbers, dates, quotes, or named events without a source the reader can check? The author's own stated work counts as a source when the page says it is theirs and gives a way to inspect it. A load-bearing particular given as external fact with no checkable source does not.

criteria.none: Specific facts are sourced, are the author's own stated work, or the page stays at a level of generality that does not invent particulars.
criteria.some: A few specifics lack a source, but they are not the main load-bearing claims.
criteria.many: Load-bearing numbers, dates, quotes, or events are given as fact with no checkable source and are not the author's own stated work.

questions.instructions: Is the text free of internal contradictions on the same fact? Two statements that agree pass. Two incompatible values for the same quantity, or a claim later denied as if it were never made, fail.

criteria.true: No two statements conflict on the same fact.
criteria.false: The page states one thing and later the opposite, for example two different values for the same quantity.

questions.instructions: Does the text match how certain it sounds to the evidence it actually shows? Strong claims need strong evidence. Personal results presented as personal results, and uncertain points that are hedged, pass. Contested or thinly supported claims stated as settled fact fail, especially in health, money, or law.

criteria.true: Strong claims come with strong evidence; uncertain points are hedged or marked as the author's view or as unknown.
criteria.false: The page states contested or thinly supported claims as settled fact, or hides strong evidence behind false uncertainty.
